articles.title: Seattle Times sues Microsoft and OpenAI, alleging they trained their AI on its journalism
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft was sued Friday by the parent company of its hometown daily newspaper, The Seattle Times Co., which joined with Newsday to accuse the Redmond tech giant and OpenAI of using their journalism to train artificial intelligence models.

The lawsuit alleges that the companies scraped hundreds of thousands of Seattle Times and Newsday articles — bypassing paywalls and ignoring terms of service — to train their AI models. It seeks financial damages and the destruction of any training datasets and models built with their content.

“Like a snake eating its own tail, GenAI that is trained on painstakingly researched, expensive-to-produce content threatens to destroy the very news organizations by competing directly with them through AI-generated substitutive content,” the suit says. “If Defendants are allowed to succeed, independent journalism of the kind Plaintiffs produce will struggle to survive.”

The case is notable in part because the Seattle Times is suing two of its own funders. Microsoft Philanthropies underwrites some Seattle Times journalism projects. In 2024, Microsoft and OpenAI jointly funded a $10 million Lenfest Institute AI fellowship that included both the Seattle Times and Newsday among its inaugural participating newsrooms. The Times says it maintains editorial independence.

A Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement Friday evening, “While we’re surprised by the lawsuit, we appreciate the importance of the Seattle Times to our region and we’re always happy to sit down and explore solutions to this type of dispute.”
It’s not clear if there were negotiations or licensing talks in advance of the suit. GeekWire has contacted The Seattle Times Co. for comment.

In its own coverage of the lawsuit Friday evening , the newspaper quoted a memo from Seattle Times Co. President and CEO Alan Fisco , saying: “This was not an easy decision. However, we feel strongly that we must defend our content — which we spend millions of dollars a year to produce — from being used without our consent or compensation.”

The Seattle Times Union, which represents more than 160 newspaper employees, said Friday it supports the lawsuit but that in ongoing contract negotiations the company has refused to guarantee it won’t replace non-reporter newsroom jobs with AI.

“If the Seattle Times Co. truly cares about the threat AI poses to journalism’s business model, it should protect the workers who produce the copyrighted material at the heart of this case,” the union said in a statement.

Fisco, a longtime Seattle Times executive, took over as CEO on Jan. 1 , succeeding Frank Blethen, who led the paper for 40 years and remains chair of the board. Ryan Blethen, Frank Blethen’s son and a fifth-generation member of the family that has owned the paper since 1896, became publisher in the same transition.

The complaint Friday includes examples of ChatGPT reproducing Seattle Times and Newsday journalism nearly word for word, including an 88-word verbatim stretch from The Seattle Times’ Pulitzer-winning coverage of the Boeing 737 MAX crashes, generated when a user prompted the chatbot with just the article’s headline and web address.

The suit echoes The New York Times’ 2023 copyright case against the same defendants, which just this week drew a U.S. Justice Department brief siding with Microsoft and OpenAI, arguing that a ruling for the publishers would stifle American AI development.

The newspapers join a growing list of publishers suing OpenAI and Microsoft over AI training. In addition to the New York Times, that includes the New York Daily News, Ziff Davis and the Center for Investigative Reporting, all consolidated before U.S. District Judge Sidney H. Stein in Manhattan.
On Friday, the publishers in that case moved for summary judgment, as did OpenAI and Microsoft.

OpenAI has struck licensing deals with more than a dozen other outlets, including The Associated Press , News Corp and Axel Springer. Publicly disclosed terms of three of those deals top $300 million, according to the Seattle Times complaint.
Updated with statement from The Seattle Times Union.

articles.title: Washington's Complete Streets Mandate Stops Short in Mukilteo
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Accessing Mukilteo's state ferry terminal, and by extension Whidbey Island and places beyond, almost always means having to navigate State Route 525. Also known as the Mukilteo Speedway, SR 525 climbs up from the Mukilteo waterfront after passing over railroad tracks that hug the shoreline, providing one of the few direct north-south routes through the city. While direct, it has limited bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure – no sidewalks and just a shoulder in the uphill direction for any cyclist who doesn't feel safe mixing with traffic.
Although a relatively recent change in state law is set to provide some upgrades, those changes are set to stop well short of the promise of full multimodal access.

State highways just like SR 525 were the intended target of a 2022 change in state law commonly referred to as the " Complete Streets Mandate ." That adjustment, tucked into the Move Ahead Washington transportation funding package, directed the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) to start planning for "facilities that provide street access with all users in mind, including pedestrians, bicyclists, and public transportation users" into all projects that cost more than $500,000, a number that was revised up to $1 million three years later.

When it passed, the Complete Streets Mandate was hailed as a sea change in highway planning in Washington State. Preservation and maintenance projects were no longer allowed to treat the status quo as the baseline to be maintained, given the fact that more than 500 miles of state highways through population centers lack pedestrian facilities, and more than 1,100 miles through population centers lack adequate bike facilities, according to WSDOT's landmark 2020 Active Transportation Plan .

Already, the mandate has changed the course of some major projects, pushing critical corridors in a much more multimodal direction. Along SR 99 through Edmonds, for example, separated bike paths were incorporated into a revamp that had been in the works before the mandate was approved, queuing up safe places to bike where they previously would have been unthinkable. But not every corridor is so lucky.

That brings us back to Mukilteo, where a repaving project that ramped up into construction this summer provides a clearer view of the Compete Streets Mandate's current shortcomings. While WSDOT is set to install several new pedestrian crossings with flashing beacons, and add a stretch of new sidewalk connecting to a bus stop, the corridor will not see bike facilities added across its entire length.

Instead, WSDOT will only install a bike lane south of 84th Street SW, a facility that will terminate just north of the juncture with the "spur" off Paine Field Bouelvard, or SR 526. That means nearly two miles out of a 2.75-mile project will remain a gap in the bike network when the project wraps up.

WSDOT project manager Tony Barilla told The Urbanist that the department was able to make room for that stretch of bike lanes by narrowing the other travel lanes and repurposing the shoulder, but that north of 84th such a move wasn't feasible without impacting the existing traffic patterns.

"Once you get closer to the ferry terminal, there is this dedicated ferry lane, so it needs to maintain that, and we don't have the shoulders, and it just really has to do with what the roadway preserves. It just wasn't feasible to narrow lanes there and remove and reallocate shoulders for infrastructure like this," Barilla said.
But the bike facilities aren't being dropped, they're instead being framed as being "deferred" in part in order to utilize a funding grant that had been set to expire.

"The paving and ADA project received a $1.5 million Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC) grant with an obligation deadline of May 2026," WSDOT's Complete Streets report on the project notes. "Full implementation of complete streets on SR 525 paving and ADA project [...] has been deferred due to the impact on project schedule and the constraint of PSRC grant obligation deadlines."

WSDOT has also established a long-term vision for SR 525, which would involve a shared-use path that transitions to two-way bike lanes all the way to the ferry terminal. But no timeline exists to be able to implement such a change.
"Everything we put in on this paving and ADA project is forward compatible. We're looking at this corridor holistically, but it is deferred until we have funding and time," Barilla said.

SR 525 is far from the only place where Complete Streets improvements are set to be deferred. Along State Route 99 in South King County, a repaving project between State Route 516 and S 272nd Street is set to add bus-only lanes and lane narrowing. But according to presentations made to the project's technical working group, WSDOT is set defer any bicycle facility component to a future date, despite the high benefits that would come from providing connectivity to Sound Transit's light rail station at Kent Des Moines Road.

WSDOT portrayed the mandate not as falling short, but providing the department with a more long-term roadmap for how to upgrade highways across the state network. But the decision whether to implement upgrades immediately along with repaving or "defer" them is one that will have a major impact on whether the mandate can truly succeed at scaling up access, or if it will happen more piecemeal.

"These are big projects to include multimodal transportation along a state highway. Complete Streets is a way to let all users use our travel facility or our roadways to travel, and so as we do projects on our state highways, and as the city does things, and as developers make new facilities, we're given a guidance of what the community wants for their multimodal transportation. And over time, through state, city, developer work, we'll get there," WSDOT spokesperson Eric Zackula told The Urbanist . "We're not here to just come in, do it, and leave. We're here for the long haul on this Complete Streets project, and and we'll get there. But we our work provides a vision, and that's what we're doing. And we're taking it bit by bit. And providing a vision for the city and also developers to to make it come true."
For bike riders just trying to get to the Mukilteo waterfront and ferry terminal, that's likely cold comfort.

articles.title: The Roundup: Should SPD Go All In on Drones?
paras: This week, we're doing things a little differently. I've been asking for submissions to "Mike's Mailbag," and I received an interesting inquiry that took some reporting to answer.

What do you think about drones for the police? After a Seattle family member had a gun battle erupt next to their house and it seemed the perpetrators were not going to be caught and I learned that other cities nearby such as Renton are allowing their police to use drones for 911 calls, I got to wondering why not SPD?

Admittedly, I wasn't aware of the Renton Police Department's drone program. The first thing I needed to do was reach out to them for a little background. Here's what I learned from the desk of Officer Michael Thompson, the drone project manager:

"The Renton Police Department started their drone program in 2015 as a result of new technology becoming available. It was introduced to the department as a way to capture more data, faster for serious collisions. At the time the traditional way of capturing data was using survey equipment and would keep roads closed for hours. The introduction of drone technology allowed for more points of data to be collected in about 30min. The department had to no longer rely on a ladder truck from the fire department to capture photos of the scene from an aerial perspective. This allowed for roads to be opened faster and more information to be collected to assist in the investigation."

Since then, the drone program has expanded, and according to Thompson, drones "are currently used in most divisions within the department." This includes patrol, where they're used the most. Pilots use drones to search for missing persons and suspects. They take photos and video of crime scenes, and SWAT uses them to sweep buildings.

Here's my simple answer for Susan: No, I don't think Seattle should adopt a drone program. Everything mentioned above sounds great, and as long as Renton continues the program as is — which, to my knowledge, is the current plan — then drones are a helpful tool. My fear is the future. Renton has already expanded the initial plan. What if it expands further? What if these drones become armed? Have you read about the way Flock cameras are being abused? Just because we can use a new tool doesn't always mean we should .

But I'm no expert — so I found someone who is. Scott Mourtgos is an assistant professor of criminology and criminal justice at the University of South Carolina. He completed the world's first study to gauge the effectiveness of drones as first responders.

Full disclosure: Mourtgos is a former cop, but he's currently an academic and isn't paid by any drone-manufacturing companies or police departments. Also, the research was done in 2025, so not all data has been compiled, and one research paper has not yet been published.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
MD: You're credited as the first person in the world to do a randomized study on drones as first responders. What does that mean, and what did you find?

SM: As far as we know, me and my research group are the first to run a randomized control trial on the outcomes of a police department using drones in a first responder program approach. You will see a lot from vendors, companies that sell drones, about success. We did an independent study.

A randomized control trial is just running a field experiment in its simplest form, using two different police departments. In one, calls were randomized on whether they received a drone response or not. In the other, the day of the week was randomized on whether drones were available to respond to calls or not.

SM: What we found, essentially across both police police departments, is that you do see a reduction in response times overall in the areas where drones are being used. We also see evidence of a workload reduction trickle-down effect, where even the calls that don't have a drone respond but are in the drone-response area and only receive a patrol officer, you see those response times reduce as well.
MD: Can drones prevent crime or contribute to public safety?

SM: There certainly is anecdotal evidence — not only at the police departments we worked with, but at other police departments — where drones overhead help everybody be more safe. Like, if you have police officers responding to an armed individual, rather than just having officers walk in blind and potentially have some sort of armed conflict, if you have a drone overhead and know exactly where that individual is and exactly what they're doing, better decisions can be made based on that information.
But I can't speak to specific outcomes just yet. We're still working on that.
MD: Based on what you've seen, would you say these drone programs are worth the cost?

SM: I can't answer that. And frankly, regardless of how much research I ever conducted on this, I would never put myself in a position where I'm telling a police department this is worth it or not worth it. Because there are so many considerations that go into whether something is worth it or not. Let's say we get to a place where we can say the specific public safety benefit to these programs — that doesn't negate possible concerns or downsides of implementing the same programs. Some people have very strong concerns about surveillance and privacy when it comes to the use of drones. I can't say how to weigh that.
MD: Great point. Reminds me of Flock cameras. Finding suspects is great, but they've also been abused. Big questions: Are all of these drones controlled by humans? Is it legal to arm these drones?

SM: Let me preface this with: I am not an attorney. But, I am not aware of any police department that has any kind of autonomous drone program. Every drone program I am aware of, and I believe the law requires this, there has to be a human operator. Until recently, they had to be within line of sight of a human. As of recently, police departments can get line of sight waivers from the FAA, where if you meet certain requirements, you no longer actually have to have human eyes on it, as far as being able to physically see it, but you're still required to have a human pilot there. I don't think it's legal to have just autonomous drones flying around doing whatever they want.

Again, caveat, I'm not a lawyer. But my understanding is that the federal law does not allow dangerous weapons to be attached to drones. I haven't seen or heard or been aware of any police departments that have even attempted to do that, let alone done that. But there is some nuance with the way that dangerous weapons are defined in federal code. Technically you could, in theory, attach a less lethal weapon to it, say a taser or some sort of pepper spray irritant or something like that. I am not aware of that happening, and a lot of jurisdictions have passed laws that ban even less than lethal weapons from being used on drones.
MD: Has this research, or any you're aware of, looked into racial disparities in drone use or the specific communities where drones are or are not used?
SM: Not that I'm aware of. We have so little research at all on drones in policing, but I'm not aware of any that addresses those questions.

articles.title: The US attorney general is fretting about a ‘pandemic’ of gender transitions in schools | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
paras: Todd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imagination

Being a public school teacher in the US these days is tough. You’ve got to pay for a lot of your own supplies, deal with smartphone-addicted children, and perform gender reassignment surgeries in your lunch break.

Luckily our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case. Blanche appeared on Fox News this week to decry a “pandemic” of gender transitions in schools across the US. “There’s not a parent in America, no matter where you live, that would want their school to change and call their child by a different name and not expect to be told about that. We partnered with the Department of Education recently to combat this very trend and, really, pandemic that’s happening in some school districts around the country,” Blanche said. He seemed more concerned with name changes than with surgery, but the president himself has suggested on several occasions that schools are furtively doing surgery on children. During a campaign speech in 2024, for example, Donald Trump said : “Can you imagine … your son leaves the house and you say: ‘Jimmy, I love you so much. Go have a good day in school,’ and your son comes back with a brutal operation? Can you even imagine this?”

articles.title: WSU President Betsy Cantwell builds custom AI agents — but won’t ask them to predict the Apple Cup
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: WSU President Betsy Cantwell is a full-on techie.

She spent more than two decades in national laboratories working on space exploration, energy and defense, followed by top leadership roles at state universities in Utah and Arizona driving significant growth in research funding. The longtime sci-fi fan embraces “future-casting” — a systems engineering approach to imagine and prepare for technological shifts a decade out.
But if that leads you to predict that the head of Washington State University is blanketing her campuses with artificial intelligence, you would be wrong.
The essential role of a university is to foster a sense of wonder in students, and that is something AI will never do, Cantwell said in a GeekWire interview on Friday.

That wonder, she said, “is innately human, and when we bring that into everything you do in a university, you create humans that will actually be much better at ideating, managing and creating value out of AI.”

In line with that philosophy, WSU faculty decide individually how to incorporate AI into their research and classrooms, with students actively involved in shaping its use. The technology serves as a tool to reach a goal, but is not the goal itself.

As the head of WSU — which serves 25,400 undergraduate and graduate students across its main campus in Pullman, four branch campuses, and an online program — Cantwell uses AI as an operational partner. On a $1.3 billion annual budget that also supports 39 county extension offices and research centers, she looks for practical AI applications to streamline functions and accelerate technology transfer.

Drawing on her national lab experience, Cantwell believes AI can bridge the gap between basic research and commercial production. Instead of universities simply “throwing papers over the transom,” she said AI-driven modeling helps build intermediate proofs-of-concept and testbeds that help attract private-sector investments.

This approach is at the foundation of WSU’s planned $50 million, federally funded research center using AI to support salmon recovery and sustainable aquaculture, as well as AI-enhanced micro-climate tools from the university to aid Washington’s farmers.
One area where Cantwell is personally using AI to guide high-stakes decision-making is in navigating the turbulent business of college athletics.

In 2023 — two years before Cantwell joined WSU — the University of Washington pulled out of the Pac-12, triggering an implosion of the century-old conference that left only WSU and Oregon State as members.

Cantwell believes strongly in the value of WSU’s athletics program, calling it a vital convener that brings alumni and fans together across political and social spectrums, while providing an academic doorway for student-athletes who might not otherwise pursue higher education.

To navigate the financial fallout, she built her own custom AI agent to run tabletop scenarios and model financial paths for WSU’s sports enterprise. She treats the exercise much like national security strategic planning.

The AI agent allows her to analyze variables including coaching salaries, stadium operations, student-athlete employment litigation, federal regulatory proposals, and revenues generated through Pac-12 Enterprises, the conference’s business arm. Cantwell sees the grit of WSU rebuilding after the Pac-12 split as a compelling story of innovation and entrepreneurship, one that new digital media channels can help broadcast.
Where Cantwell draws the line, however, is AI use in sports betting, which she views as a concerning manipulation of human behavior that threatens the integrity of college athletics.

GeekWire came prepared for our interview by asking different AI chatbots to predict the outcome of Sunday’s Apple Cup showdown between WSU and UW at Seattle’s Husky Stadium. Suffice to say, the AI says it doesn’t look good for the squad from the Palouse.
But before we could deliver that news, the top Cougar made it clear she wasn’t interested in hearing what Gemini, Claude or any other AI platform forecast for the game.
“The only reason why I would want to know the score in advance is if I was betting and I don’t do that,” Cantwell said. “Why do you need to know in advance?”

articles.title: ‘Sonic the Hedgehog’ exhibit makes a weekend run in Seattle, with fan art and 35 years of history
articles.author: Thomas Wilde
paras: If you attended the Sunset Market in Seattle’s Pioneer Square on Thursday night, you might’ve noticed that one of the local galleries had been transformed into a shrine to, of all things, Sonic the Hedgehog.

That’s because on Labor Day weekend, Seattle is hosting 35 Years of Speed: The Sonic Art Exhibit. This touring art collection is part of the celebration of the anniversary of the Sonic franchise, which began in 1991 with the original Sonic the Hedgehog for the Sega Genesis.

The Sonic Art Exhibit features framed concept and box art from the Sonic archives, several pieces by official Sonic artists, and a curated selection of pieces created and submitted by the Sonic fan community, which includes paintings, sketches, and even statuary.

“It’s Sonic’s 35th anniversary, so we’ve been looking at ways to celebrate his legacy,” said Jessica Perri, Sega brand director. “We commissioned 50-plus artists across styles and different mediums, and we also worked with fans who bring their own inspirations to the table. We’re displaying it all here in Seattle over the course of the weekend.”
Perri continued, “We’re really just excited to celebrate Sonic through the lens of art.”

The game was Sega’s first-party “killer app,” intended to compete directly with the Super Nintendo and its Super Mario franchise. The title character is a blue hedgehog with the power of super-speed, who fights alongside his friends against his nemesis, Dr. Ivo Robotnik.
In the last 35 years, Sonic has appeared in more than 100 video games, which range from some absolute classics to one of the most infamous misfires in the history of the medium.

There have also been multiple lines of merchandise; several animated shows; a successful live-action film series with a fourth entry coming in early 2027; a popular comic book, which is currently published by San Diego-based IDW; and a recent comic crossover with the DC Universe that did well enough to get a sequel . (Trivia: Sonic the Hedgehog is now technically a member of the Justice League.)

35 Years of Speed: The Sonic Art Exhibit is running at Seattle’s 210 Gallery at 301 Occidental Ave. S. from Sept. 4 through Sept. 6 from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Admission is free. After its Seattle run, the exhibition will have its final show in Los Angeles later this month.

articles.title: Startup Spotlight: Food photographer uses 25-year archive to build an AI tool that eliminates costly reshoots
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Longtime Seattle food photographer Scott Pitts spent 25 years capturing commercial imagery for major brands, and now he’s using that quarter-century archive to train Pallat . The new AI-powered production system is designed to eliminate costly reshoots while keeping real studio craft at the center of generative creative tech.

The platform combines fine-tuned open-weight models with Pitts’ extensive archive, allowing art directors to modify existing campaign assets — like swapping a topping, adjusting lighting, or changing a backdrop — in minutes through software rather than starting from scratch back on set.

Pitts, a non-technical founder operating Pallat out of his Seattle photo studio, SP Studio , leads a nimble five-person team and believes domain experience is key to competing with generic AI platforms.
“We are close to the problem, and we’re looking at it from a photographic eye,” he said. “We’re making sure those outputs look photoreal, that they’re not going to get labeled as AI slop.”

To show how the tech works in practice, Pitts points to a recent shoot for a national steakhouse client. After completing a complex setup for a burger — carefully layering the bun, patty, sauce, and greens — the brand asked if they had shot a version with tomatoes. Rather than calling back the food stylist and rebuilding the set, Pitts dropped the final image into Pallat, prompting it to add two tomato slices with subtle condensation, natural translucency, and accurate drop shadows cast onto the cheese below.

In another instance, a commercial seafood brand prepared packaging imagery for a buyer presentation, only for the client to ask to see the fish presented on a white plate instead. Pallat to the rescue.

Commercial photographers have long tweaked images using tools like Photoshop, but Pitts sees AI as the natural next step for advertising workflows — distinct from news photography, where image manipulation remains out of bounds. Where Photoshop requires painstaking manual editing to adjust a scene, Pallat handles complex lighting, translucency, and material physics in minutes based on a simple prompt.
The startup recently signed its first enterprise customer and is currently working directly with brands as a hands-on production partner while building toward full software access.

Pitts sees the technology not as a threat to his craft, but as a natural progression. He started his career shooting four-by-five film, then transitioned to digital and video. AI is another progression.
“My hope is that me building Pallat is sort of this bridge between tech and creative,” Pitts said. “Craft is still important. Judgment and taste are still probably some of the most important things.”
Continue reading for Pitts’ answers to our Startup Spotlight questionnaire.
In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

Pallat is a photographer-led AI production system built for food and beverage brands, born from a working photo studio. It combines licensed photography with generative workflows to help brands scale photo-centric content while maintaining the creative control expected from commercial photography.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?

I’ve spent 25 years watching brands solve the same problem: invest in a shoot, then ultimately need more usable imagery than the initial shoot was designed to deliver. Generic generative tools can create images, but weren’t built around the quality, control and production standards food and beverage brands require.

I’m obsessed with using AI to close the gap. Pallat gives brands a way to extend photography they’ve already invested in and create new production-ready imagery grounded in a licensed dataset and the standards of a traditional photoshoot.
What surprised you after talking to customers?
Because we’re so close to the problem we’re solving, their need for a solution and high bar for quality didn’t surprise me.

What did was how much generated imagery disrupted their existing workflows. There is no obvious owner, no review path and no shared vocabulary for feedback and approvals. Brands are asking us to help establish new workflows, and that has turned out to be almost as important as building the tech itself.
How has AI changed the way you build your company?

AI is a big part of why a five-person team can build something like this. Our tech stack is built on open-weight models that we fine-tune using proprietary training data, while foundation models support planning and a handful of day-to-day operations.

Not to oversimplify it, but in many ways my role at Pallat parallels production. I built a team of experts, defined the problem we’re solving and established the criteria for the output. A growing part of my work is getting those standards out of my head and structuring evals so they hold when I’m not in the room.
What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?
That Pallat is trying to replace photography. It’s far from it.

Practical photos are important inputs, and our studio continues to create net-new ones to expand the system. Visual trends are always evolving, so datasets powering creative tech cannot be static. The future of production is hybrid: practical photography and generative imaging working together, with each deployed where it creates the most value.
What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Resisting the urge to broaden Pallat before we establish product-market fit. The goal isn’t to automate every step as quickly as possible. It’s to understand which problems in the workflow are best solved through software.
What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

I truly believe some of the most interesting AI companies will come out of service businesses where the founder knows the industry exceptionally well — where the friction lives, which shortcuts a client will notice, and what excellence looks like in their vertical.

I spent a long time assuming my 25 years in photography was the past and AI was the future, and I had that backwards. The years on set that sharpened my taste and judgment, our dataset and the client relationships are the true compounding assets.
When an art director at a food or beverage brand drafts a shot list dividing it into two columns: “Capture as Practical Photography” and “Generate in Pallat.”
When that becomes a normal way of planning, Pallat will have done what we set out to do.

articles.title: Etzioni on AI: What kids tell chatbots, but not you
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: Kids are heading back to school across the country with a tool in their pocket that will do their homework, answer the questions they’re too embarrassed to ask an adult, and never tell anyone they asked.

MIT Technology Review asked kids aged 10 to 18 what they make of AI. Their answers had me plowing through every survey and interview with kids about AI I could find. Plenty of what kids do with it is ordinary: looking things up, homework, messing around.
This article is about the parts they keep to themselves.
1. Kids are taking their mental health to a chatbot, and telling nobody .
Nearly one in five Americans aged 12 to 21 has asked a chatbot for help when feeling sad, angry or nervous. RAND puts it at 8.2 million young people, and 63% of them told no one at all.
The silence is a calculation about what adults would do, as one teenager explained to YouGov’s researchers .
The most vulnerable kids use chatbots more.
Some teenagers see AI as a shortcut past the hard parts of schoolwork.
Others describe using it the opposite way.

Between May and December 2025, RAND watched homework use among middle school, high school and college students climb from 48% to 62%. Over a slightly longer stretch, from February, the share saying AI harms critical thinking climbed from 54% to 67%. The same students can hold both thoughts at once.

The Concord Monitor interviewed eight New Hampshire high schoolers this spring. They weren’t outraged at their classmates, but they described losing motivation to do the work themselves. One in ten teens tells Pew they do all or most of their schoolwork with a chatbot’s help.
Caledonia Mahon, a Concord High senior, watched a classmate stand up and admit he’d had ChatGPT write a personal reflection, and started wondering why she was still writing her own.
Her classmate Andrew Pfitzenmayer supplied the detail I can’t get out of my head, about a boy in his advanced history class.
Yet, the same technology can be positive for kids who don’t have much else.

By May 2025, 84% of American high schoolers were using AI for schoolwork at least occasionally. The kids who lean on it hardest have the least support around them, which is why telling them to quit doesn’t work.
If quitting isn’t the option, what’s left is changing what the tool does when a kid opens it. Two Seattle startups are trying that.
3. Kids are writing the rules adults haven’t .
Suspicion of AI runs strongest among the kids furthest from it: 78% of students who don’t use AI say it harms critical thinking, against 60% of those who do.

In July, 98 high schoolers from all 50 states spent three days in a replica of the U.S. Senate chamber in Boston and passed what Congress hasn’t. Their STUDENTS FIRST Act requires AI literacy, bars teachers from letting AI decide a grade on its own, lets a teacher ask a student to defend suspected work out loud, and gives any student the right to an alternative to an AI assignment.

A majority of educators told Education Week’s Research Center last fall that their district has no AI policy, or that they don’t know whether it does. At least seven states have a comprehensive one, by Education Week’s count.

Ashley Kannan has taught social studies for almost 30 years in Oak Park, Ill. He planned to ignore AI, then noticed that every conversation about it in his building was about catching students. He recruited nine eighth graders to spend a year working out what AI was actually good for. In April they briefed 60+ teachers and parents on the rules they thought were needed.

Hazel is 17 , a rock climber in New York who wants to be an ecologist. She won’t touch AI, and her reason is specific: what data centers do to the water supplies of the towns they’re built in. Asked what advice she’d give other kids, she gave four words.
Hazel can afford that advice. Most kids can’t.

So the practical alternative is narrower than just telling them to quit: ask them what they use AI for, ask what they’ve decided not to use it for, and don’t make an honest answer cost them the tool. Right now 61% of young people say their parents rarely or never talk to them about AI, and 53% say the same of their teachers.
Hazel may walk away from AI. But Amira, describing a pain in her side to a chatbot, may not, and the odds are nobody in her house knows she’s doing it.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Race the L8 again… and lose?
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: The L8 is not so late anymore since an eastbound traffic lane was converted to a bus lane in August. On Tuesday, September 8th , Fix the L8 is organizing another race against Metro’s bus Route 8 along Denny Way. Unlike the previous event , the group is expecting to lose as the buses bypass traffic via newly-painted eastbound bus lanes.

“Across multiple decades and several mayors, it’s been obvious that a bus lane is needed on Denny Way, and it only took a few months of Mayor Wilson’s leadership to get one” said Fix The L8 co-leader Jason Li. “This will transform the lives of the thousands of daily Route 8 riders while attracting countless more as it goes from being slower than hopscotching to being irresistibly good.”

Other traffic improvements, including closure of the Yale Street slip lane, have also helped speed up the bus. Although transit projects are often mired in years of design and debate, it’s abundantly clear that concerted effort and leadership can shorten this work to mere months. In this case, Mayor Katie Wilson requested accelerated design and construction of the transit prioritization project as her first executive order in January of this year. The improvements were announced in April and the project completed at the end of August .
Riders were quick to notice a vast improvement:

Despite the international media coverage focused on the impact this bus lane would have on drivers, travel times between Queen Anne Ave to Virginia St for cars has remained consistent. The chart below shows the estimated eastbound travel time for a car along the 1.1 mile segment of Denny way at the top of every hour since early July. The stripped blue section is the after the Yale St slip lane was closed in early August. The bus lanes were installed between August 21-23. Explore the full chart here .
The rematch race will begin at 5pm next Tuesday. Anyone interested is encouraged to RSVP to the event, here . The race will be followed by a celebratory gathering at The Pine Box in Capitol Hill.

The Fix the L8 campaign is also taking preorders of a tremendously-cute, limited-edition Route 8 plushie with first shipments expected to arrive in early October. The bus plushie (a busie!) is endorsed by STB as a perfect gift for the upcoming holiday season. Order yours here ! Proceeds go toward future campaigns for transit and street safety improvements.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Brian Heywood’s Plan to Take Over Snohomish County Government Must Be Stopped
articles.author: Andrew Villeneuve (Guest Contributor)
paras: This autumn, at the same time that Washington voters will be deciding the fate of three destructive statewide initiatives from wealthy hedge fund mogul Brian Heywood, Snohomish County voters will face a slate of proposed changes to the county’s plan of government. The measures were submitted by a Republican-controlled, Heywood-aligned charter review commission.

They’re the centerpiece of a multiyear Republican plan to take over the government of Snohomish County, Washington’s third-largest jurisdiction… a plan that Democrats, progressives, and urbanists have yet to prioritize countering. This is Heywood’s other ballot play this year, and it’s one many people haven’t heard about.

There are five propositions in all. Two of the five have been explicitly engineered to help Republicans win elections and control the county’s fiscal trajectory, regardless of whether they ever win a council majority:
Should these propositions pass, Republicans will be well positioned to execute the final stage of their takeover plan in 2027 and begin gaining control of Snohomish County’s government.
While 37 of Washington’s 39 counties elect their county leadership in even-numbered years, Snohomish and Whatcom schedule most of those same elections in odd-numbered years.

King County used to do likewise, but in 2022, voters approved a charter amendment developed by my team at the Northwest Progressive Institute and sponsored by Councilmember Claudia Balducci that began moving King County elections to even-numbered years.

Five men have served as Snohomish County executive since voters adopted the county’s first charter: Willis Tucker (1980–1992), Bob Drewel (1992–2004), Aaron Reardon (2004–2013), John Lovick (2013–2016), and Dave Somers (2016–present).
Every one of them has won election as a Democrat. In nearly half a century of charter government, Republicans have never elected one of their candidates to the county’s top job.

Somers cannot run again in 2027 because he is nearing the end of his third consecutive term and the executive is limited to three terms . Consequently, Snohomish County will have its first open race for executive since 2003, and multiple Democrats are known to be interested.

Republicans see a once-in-a-generation opportunity to exploit Democratic divisions and elect a Republican executive. With the Republican brand badly damaged by Donald Trump’s regime and its base’s embrace of White Christian nationalism , Republicans reckon they will have a better chance of gaining power in Snohomish County if candidates are barred from placing a party label beside their names on the ballot.

Republicans have already recently proven they can win a major county contest when there are no party labels next to the candidates’ names. In 2019, extreme right-wing candidate Adam Fortney defeated incumbent Sheriff Ty Trenary with 55.4% of the vote . Although Fortney’s tenure was disastrous, reformer Susanna Johnson only narrowly defeated him in 2023, 51.5% to 48.4% .

Neighboring King County is a deep blue bastion, but Snohomish is more purple. It usually votes Democratic, but its electorate is very different from King County’s. For example, King County leaders can send the voters they represent a levy in almost any election and be confident it has excellent odds of passing. Snohomish County leaders cannot do that. Sales and property tax increases are a tough sell in Snohomish.
The Republican Party already has a prospective candidate for executive with a countywide profile: Nate Nehring.

Along with Sam Low, Nehring is one of two incumbent Republican county councilmembers. Nehring is sitting on an eye-popping $359,673 in surplus campaign cash , according to Public Disclosure Commission data, and is well positioned to raise more because he has served as the Snohomish County director of Brian Heywood’s Future 42.

Nehring’s surplus cash cannot automatically move into an executive campaign. When a candidate switches to running for a different position, state law requires written permission from the original contributors , and approved transfers count toward each contributor’s limit in the new race. Nevertheless, the surplus war chest and the donor network behind Nehring are formidable assets.

Future 42 is the connective tissue of this entire operation. It is a project of Project 42, a 501(c)(4) nonprofit that identifies Heywood as a co-founder . IRS records list Heywood as vice chair and secretary . A Project 42 event page says contributions are unlimited and donors are not disclosed.
The Cascadia Daily News reported that Project 42 seeks “durable conservative infrastructure” and chose Snohomish County because it considers the county politically competitive.
Future 42’s County Council scorecard targets general and road-fund property-tax increases, a housing and behavioral-health capital plan, critical-areas regulations, and other local issues.

Future 42 and League of Our Own Washington, another Heywood-backed group, say they recruited or trained more than 90 local candidates in 2025. Afterward, Future 42 claimed more than 60 victories , including an 11-of-15 “supermajority” on the Snohomish County Charter Review Commission.

With that supermajority, Republicans were able to send five charter amendments to voters. The two at the heart of the takeover plan draw from a familiar Washington Republican playbook: in 2008, future state senator and Bellevue Chamber CEO Joe Fain sponsored a successful county initiative to strip party labels from King County ballots, while in the 1990s and 2000s, Linda Smith and Tim Eyman hawked unconstitutional statewide measures designed to make state taxes harder to raise, which were followed by a number of copycat measures at the county and city levels.

If Nehring wins countywide and Republicans later flip District 4 (or, alternatively, Districts 2 or 3, though those are much more Democratic), they could control both the executive and legislative branches of county government as of the beginning of 2028, assuming Nehring’s District 1 council seat was filled by another Republican.
The consequences of this takeover would extend far beyond the county courthouse.

The county executive occupies one of Snohomish County’s three seats on the 18-member Sound Transit Board and chooses the other two representatives. State law makes those appointments subject to County Council confirmation and gives boardmembers staggered four-year terms. Winning the executive’s office therefore provides one board vote immediately and the power to shape the rest of the delegation as terms turn over.
Flipping the council would also give Republicans the majority needed to confirm those choices.
Readers of The Urbanist know how important the decisions made by the Sound Transit Board are.

The board chooses which alternatives receive environmental review, selects preferred alignments and station locations, adopts project budgets, establishes scope and schedule baselines, and approves major contracts.

Major decisions require a two-thirds vote , making a cohesive three-member county delegation capable of helping assemble — or deny — a regional supermajority. The board will exercise that power while attempting to close a $34.5 billion long-term funding gap .

The future of regionwide Sound Transit 3 (ST3) expansion, including Everett Link, will be affected by this year’s charter amendment votes and next year’s county elections. The board will decide what gets built north of Lynnwood, when it opens, where stations go, and how much of the voter-approved line survives the affordability crisis.

Community Transit (CT) will also be affected by the 2026 and 2027 elections. CT is an independent public transportation benefit area, not a county department, and its Board of Directors sets policy, approves the budget, and hires and supervises the agency’s chief executive. The county executive has no automatic seat and cannot dictate routes, fares, or service levels. But two of Community Transit’s nine voting board seats are held by Snohomish County councilmembers selected by the County Council.

Those seats are currently held by Democrats Megan Dunn and Strom Peterson. Because state law says directors serve at the pleasure of the governing bodies that select them, a Republican council majority could replace Dunn and Peterson with two Republican councilmembers, gaining direct votes over Community Transit’s budget, service priorities, and capital program. The remaining seven voting directors are selected by cities, so the county seats alone would not provide control of the agency.

Even without controlling Community Transit, a Republican executive and council could shape the environment in which it operates. County decisions determine land use and road design throughout unincorporated Snohomish County, including transit-priority treatments, traffic signals, sidewalks and crossings that provide access to bus stops, and potential park-and-ride locations. Capital partnerships can also require interlocal agreements with county governments.

A Republican takeover would therefore give the party both two direct board votes and substantial leverage over whether county infrastructure helps or hinders fast, reliable, and accessible bus service.

Republican control would also put both sides of local land-use governance (making the rules and carrying them out) in the same party’s hands. The council adopts the comprehensive plan, zoning and development regulations, and operating and capital budgets. The executive supervises the departments that draft and administer those plans, process permits, maintain county roads, and deliver housing and human services.
Those powers will shape how Snohomish County accommodates extraordinary growth.

The county’s 2044 planning framework is built around countywide targets of 1,136,309 residents and 467,634 jobs. Local decisions will help determine whether that growth produces abundant homes in walkable, transit-rich communities or more displacement, sprawl, and car dependence.

The stakes are most concrete in the unincorporated urban core between Everett, Mill Creek, Lynnwood, and Mukilteo. The county is considering a Light Rail Community zone for 983 acres around the future Ash Way, Mariner, and provisional SR 99/Airport Road stations. The current proposal would establish a minimum density of 50 homes per acre, remove maximum residential densities, reduce parking mandates, and require 15% of units in qualifying developments to be affordable. Even if the council adopts those rules this year, the next executive and council will oversee their implementation and could revisit the development code.

County budgets and transportation plans determine whether growing communities receive sidewalks, safe crossings, bicycle connections, ADA ramps, parks, road designs that support transit, and the local matching dollars that unlock state and federal grants.

A Republican executive and council could prioritize roadway expansion and car throughput over safer streets and transit access; weaken affordable-housing and anti-displacement work; redirect resources from homelessness programs; or push more growth toward the suburban and rural fringe. The Growth Management Act and state housing laws constrain some choices, but they leave substantial discretion in county hands.

Nehring has already offered a concrete preview of how he would govern. In 2024, he proposed freezing the county’s general property-tax levy and paying for it through a sweeping package of budget cuts that would have reduced Sheriff’s Office budget lines by more than $1.07 million a year, imposed broad reductions throughout county government, and cut funding for public defense, court interpretation, juvenile electronic monitoring and nursing, Medical Examiner testing, parks maintenance, emergency management, and several county positions. Sheriff Susanna Johnson warned that the proposal could cost as many as 18 budgeted but then-vacant positions .
Proposition 5 is a complementary long-term play for Republicans.

articles.title: Seattle Will Spend $350K to Fund Community Passageways Street Team in Rainier Beach Through June 2027
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson announced on Aug. 29 that the City was committed to providing $350,000 in funding for Community Passageways' Southeast Street Team in Rainier Beach until June 2027.

The announcement, which Wilson made at the Rainier Beach Community Center, came after months of organizing from Rainier Beach parents and community groups to save funding for the team. More than 40 people, including parents, organizers, city officials, officers with the Seattle Police Department (SPD), and representatives of various violence-interrupter groups, were at the center.

At a community meeting held earlier this summer, numerous parents voiced frustration with City officials over the anticipated end to a contract that funded Community Passageways' street team in Rainier Beach. At the time, one parent called it "another death for the kids."

Seattle's Human Services Department (HSD) is still finalizing the agreement with Community Passageways, but in an email to the Emerald , an HSD representative wrote that the anticipated agreement will provide approximately $350,000 in "one-time funding" to cover the Southeast Street Team through June 30, 2027.

The funding will support six staff members, with the scope of the agreement covering "Safe Passage, outreach, and violence-prevention coverage in the Rainier Beach corridor from approximately 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m." HSD also confirmed the funding would "complement" the work of a cohort of 19 other community-based providers in "delivering services and building relationships with young people, families, schools, and neighborhoods across Seattle."

In an email, the Mayor's Office did not specify where the $350,000 will come from. The City of Seattle is currently facing a $175 million budget deficit. Earlier this summer, City Councilmember Maritza Rivera said funding for public safety programs should be addressed in the upcoming budget cycle.

After the funding announcement was made, attendees expressed pride in their successful organizing efforts and were excited the street team would be funded for the upcoming school year. "At the end of the day, community has power," said Community Passageways CEO Dominique Davis.
Davis, with his arm around Wilson, said, "Katie, thank you for caring about our kids. We appreciate you."

Wilson, in her speech, discussed the work Community Passageways does to prevent youth gun violence and the relationships the organization builds. "Part of what makes [Rainier Beach] great are all the relationships," said Wilson. She also acknowledged that "the City hasn't always shown up" in South Seattle, but funding for Community Passageways is a first step toward ongoing work in the area to address gun violence.

In recent weeks, Wilson has focused attention on the South End, including attending the recent "Night Out" event in Rainier Beach and prioritizing traffic safety projects along dangerous roads, such as Rainier Avenue South and Martin Luther King Jr. Way South.

One parent, who spoke to the audience at the community center, acknowledged the traffic safety projects in South Seattle, but said it feels "irresponsible" to let the kids walk or bike outside because of the gun violence.

Many parents spoke in support of the work Community Passageways does, including one who said they "witnessed the earned trust of the street team." They added, "We deserve consistency." HSD wrote in an email that the funding for Community Passageways was not only to continue building those relationships but also to provide "consistent coverage" in South Seattle.
Another parent told Wilson that funding Community Passageways will "pay dividends; we just need to make sure everyone has an equal chance."

Although the parents and organizers celebrated the funding, the consensus was that there is more work to do. Community members said they want greater investments in preventing youth gun violence, including funding for Community Passageways after 2027, as well as Community Passageways school-based staff to return to Rainier Beach.
Parents and organizers also encouraged Wilson to meet with young people in South Seattle.

Currently, Community Passageways contracts with the City for hospital-based intervention, citywide support services, work in the Central District, and school-based services. Along with the street team, Community Passageways also operates diversion and mentorship programs for youth and young adults.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, September 7–September 13
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Shannon Lubetich, Amanda Manitach, Emily Nokes, and Langston Thomas
paras: (MUSIC) For Seattleites, Death Cab for Cutie needs no introduction. Frontman Ben Gibbard started the indie rock band nearly three decades ago while attending Western Washington University. Since then, they’ve released 11 studio albums and won the adoration of listeners all over the world thanks to their catchy and emotional tracks. This weekend, the group headlines Bumbershoot before taking off on a European tour in support of their recent release, I Built You a Tower . But before they do, they’re stopping by KEXP to perform for some of their earliest supporters. I recommend getting to the venue early, grabbing a drink from Caffe Vita, enjoying the on-air DJ’s tunes, and staking out a spot in line for the free event before the Labor Day crowd catches up! I’m expecting the in-studio performance to feel like the Pacific Northwest homecoming version of Death Cab’s recent Tiny Desk concert . ( KEXP, 11 am, free, all ages ) SHANNON LUBETICH

(COMMUNITY) Last year, in an attempt to highlight the absurdity of King County Metro’s 8 bus line, the grassroots volunteer group Fix the L8 hosted an event called “Race the L8.” Participants successfully proved that several alternate modes of transportation, such as walking, leap-frogging, cha-cha-sliding, conga lining, and hopscotching, were all faster than the perpetually tardy bus. Now that Mayor Wilson has installed bus-only lanes on Denny Way, they’re testing it again to see if—gasp—the 8 can actually beat the racers this time. Wilson, a Route 8 bus driver, and Fix the L8 leads will deliver brief remarks, followed by a race along the southern sidewalk of Denny/Stewart and a happy hour at the Pine Box. ( Denny and Dexter, 5 pm, free ) JULIANNE BELL

(FILM) There’s nothing else I can say about Dolly Parton that hasn’t already been said, written, or shouted from the rooftops in the past week. But rather than grieve, it seems most are choosing to celebrate her storied life and career, and that includes the folks at the Northwest Film Forum. This Friday, they’ll pay tribute with a screening of The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas (1982), starring Parton as Miss Mona, the proprietor of a Texas brothel threatened by a crusading TV personality, with Burt Reynolds playing the sheriff (and love interest). It’s a big, boisterous musical that’s about as fittingly Dolly as a memorial screening could get. Plus, NWFF is turning it into a proper celebration, with a special pre-show kicking things off at 7 pm. ( Northwest Film Forum, 7:30 pm ) LANGSTON THOMAS

(VISUAL ART) Meghan Thréinfhir ’s sculptural and conceptual work does a lot of heavy lifting, blending cosmic physics, computing, and witchcraft. For more than a decade, she’s been working with the bog—yes, actual, wet, earthy bog—to create sonic electrical installations and other mind-bending sculptures that allow us to enter a space where ancient planetary physics and contemporary technology coexist. For her solo exhibit at Steve Gilbert Studio , SPACETIME GOTHIC , Thréinfhir presents work about black holes and the accretion discs that form around their perimeter, imagining the orbiting material as a ghostly sort of library at the edge of the void—a place where matter may be lost but information is never destroyed. ( Steve Gilbert Studio, free, all ages ) AMANDA MANITACH

(PERFORMANCE) There are few comedians you could identify from delivery and voice alone quite as quickly as Anthony Jeselnik. His slow, deliberate cadence practically announces that something terrible is about to come out of his mouth. And, more often than not, it does. Jeselnik has spent the past 25 years perfecting his particular brand of dark humor, from breakout appearances roasting Charlie Sheen and Donald Trump to specials like Thoughts and Prayers , Fire in the Maternity Ward , and 2024’s Bones and All . Granted, Jeselnik’s sense of dark humor isn’t for everyone… But a room full of cynical Seattleites? That’s essentially his target demographic. ( Moore Theatre, 7:30 pm, all ages ) LANGSTON THOMAS

(PERFORMANCE) The Genius Awards is a ceremony where we give six big-ass checks to Geniuses of Film, Food, Literature, Music, Performance, and Visual Art! There will be drag (the event is hosted by Miss Texas 1988 and Lady GuGu), there will be DJs (past Genius Award-winner Erik Blood is in town; La Mala Noche closes the evening with a basement dance party 10–11 p.m.), there will be trophies (handmade by local art wizard Mary Anne Carter). Past Genius Award winners Shabazz Palaces will headline; their lead single “Ahh World (I Won The Alpha Bet)” off their excellent upcoming album, It’s a Style Sport , says to “put your money where your mouth is”—our thoughts exactly. A party, a ceremony, a show, all in the name of CELEBRATING ART. What more could you want for 10 bucks? Speaking of style, do you have a special or weird thing in your closet that you never get to bust out? Now is the time! Personally, I’m aiming for something between an opulent magician and Miss Scarlet from the 1985 Clue movie. ( Moore Theatre, 6:30 pm, all ages ) EMILY NOKES

(FILM) I’m a simple woman: If a film stars Bette Davis, I’ll watch it. That’s how I came to find out about The Little Foxes , the 1941 drama based on Southern leftist playwright Lillian Hellman’s 1939 play of the same name (which the Intiman Theatre staged last fall). Davis plays the ambitious, ruthless ice queen Regina Hubbard Giddens, who goes head to head with her morally bankrupt brothers and principled husband in her quest for wealth. As one Letterboxd reviewer put it, it’s “basically old-timey Succession,” complete with its own Cousin Greg. Rick Burin of The Guardian called it a “visually astounding leftwing polemic that climaxes with the best horror sequence of its decade” and referred to Giddens as “a psychopath who presages the next 79 years of rapacious capitalism.” No one plays a complete psycho bitch better than Davis. ( Beacon Cinema, 6 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

articles.title: I Have the Best and Craziest 7 Bus Story Ever
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: The storied Route 7 now has an expiration date: 2032 . At that point, King County Metro will change it to RapidRide R Line, a bus that will run between Rainier Beach and downtown Seattle. This new line will require the transformation of Rainier Avenue, a former highway with a reputation for fast cars that regularly crash into buildings, poles, and people .

Route 7 also has a bad reputation: Its buses are often so late that they get clustered—you have massive gaps between no bus at all and two or three buses arriving all at once. The situation, which hasn’t much improved since the introduction of some bus-only lanes in 2022, was even worse when the 7 ran from Rainier Beach to the University District, with stops in downtown and Capitol Hill. Those dismal days, the ones before Route 49 began service in 2005 , experienced useless clusters of four to five Route 7 buses.

But I still love the 7. It’s the people’s bus. And not only that, it’s the Asian/Black/Latino bus. It’s not infrequent that one takes the 7 and finds the only white person on the bus is the driver. This route is minority majority on wheels, even to this day, despite the considerable gentrification of large sections of South Seattle. The 7 keeps it real; it remains faithful to the city’s historically most diverse area , Rainier Valley. But this diversity is not just racial. It’s also about characters. The reason why the 7 has so many great stories is because it serves so many different types of personalities, some of which are, for sure, very unusual.

It was on a Route 7 bus that I experienced one of the strangest characters in my life. This incident happened some eight years ago, and around the point the bus leaves Rainier and turns into Little Saigon.

That day, the trip between Columbia City (where I live) and Little Saigon had been unusually uninteresting. But that all changed when we got to the stop by the Boat, an iconic Vietnamese restaurant. For some reason, the doors at the back of the bus were jammed. And a man (short, mixed-race, and full of something that was eating his mind) kept screaming at the driver to “OPEN THE BACK DOOR!” It was like his whole life depended upon it. But the door would, again and again, partially open and then abruptly shut. And with each failure, the man’s heat and voice would rise with greater force: “OPEN THE BACK DOOR!!!!!”

The insanely intense temperature of this man rattled the nerves of everyone in the back of the bus, which included its only white person: a woman who appeared to be a college student. She had blondish hair and bluish eyes that disclosed her growing fear of the screaming man. The door yet again attempted to open and failed. But before the man’s head exploded, a middle-aged Black man (who reminded me a little of Howlin’ Wolf) dressed in dungerees stood, rushed to the door, and rationally determined the problem: the door was jammed by an abandoned Coca-Cola can. He picked it up, and the door finally and smoothly opened, and the fury left the bus to lord knows where.

The young white woman, relieved that the end of the world was over, turned to her enlightened savior in the dungarees and thanked him profusely for resolving this chaotic situation. He calmly looked at her for a moment. Raised his eyebrows. And began barking. Like a dog. A very big dog. One that was neither aggressive nor friendly. She was totally stunned. He did not speak human. He only barked. And sounded like a Great Dane or maybe a Bullmastiff. In either case, the barking was so convincing that it was hard to believe a human throat and mouth produced it.

The whole back of the bus was also stunned by the hound man in the dungarees, who returned to his seat barking to himself. The look on the white woman’s face said it all: What planet am I on? In what world does a person perfect the cry of a dog? Only the 7, baby.

articles.title: How a Great Director Made a Very Bad Film That He Is Proud Of
articles.author: Kathy Fennessy
paras: British director John Boorman had already made six movies before he got the chance to direct Exorcist II: The Heretic , the 1977 sequel to William Friedkin’s 1973 blockbuster about demonic possession, The Exorcist . Boorman was hardly a novice. He even had two stone-cold classics, Point Blank and Deliverance , to his name.

But in making a movie about hope and goodness, in which Linda Blair’s former victim becomes a sort of psychic healer, Boorman disappointed those expecting more head swivels, green goo, and blasphemous “yo mama” jokes.

As director David Kittredge (Shudder’s docuseries Queer for Fear: The History of Queer Horror ) makes clear in his affectionate and contextually rich new documentary, Boorman and the Devil, about what the director describes as “one of the most famous failures of all time in the cinema,” Boorman was a wild card who never made the same film twice.

His directorial debut, Catch Us If You Can , for instance, was a satirical vehicle for British invaders the Dave Clark Five, whereas the apocalyptic sci-fi fantasy Zardoz remains best known for Sean Connery’s red fetish-wear mankini and the immortal phrase, “The gun is good, the penis is evil!”

In Boorman and the Devil , the director, 85 at the time, appears at his home in Ireland with a model of the stone Zardoz idol head behind him, indicating fondness for a film that no one knew what to make of in 1974. That would also be the case with The Heretic , his preferred title, since he saw his 1977 film more as a “riposte” than a sequel.

Kittredge’s documentary brims with frank interviews with cast and crew, cleverly-edited film clips, and playful illustrations, but his ace in the hole are Boorman’s unromantic, clear-eyed recollections.

“It made oceans of money for Warner’s, but I didn’t enjoy it,” he says of The Exorcist . He did enjoy playwright William Goodhart’s treatment for The Heretic , which called on Goodhart’s expertise with theology and the occult, and that’s what led to his participation (original author William Peter Blatty, who directed the second sequel, The Exorcist III , was not involved).

From here, all went downhill, and everything that could go wrong did. He persuaded Linda Blair and Max von Sydow to return, but Ellen Burstyn passed and Lee J. Cobb, who played homicide detective Kinderman in the first film, died of a heart attack. He cast other fine actors, like Louise Fletcher, who had just won the Oscar for One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest , and Kitty Winn from The Panic in Needle Park . They did what they could, but the results pleased almost no one, and yet this isn’t a sad or tragic tale, because most everyone actually enjoyed working on this glorious mess.

It is, instead, a way of looking at Boorman’s career through the lens of his biggest bomb, because it was an innovative film with heady ideas about metaphysical communication and stunning practical effects, like a daring sequence in which Blair walks to the edge of an NYC high-rise and a horde of 3,000 real-deal locusts. It was also emblematic of 1970s filmmaking, because he had a ride-or-die crew and money to burn. But the project was cursed, as it were, by an ever-changing script, deadly disease, and a studio-mandated lead, Richard Burton, fresh off a triumphant run in Peter Shaffer’s play Equus , with no appetite for the material.

But failure has a way of revealing an artist’s true colors, and Boorman, now 93, didn’t let the experience break him. Instead, he got back up, dusted himself off, and continued to make the kinds of films he wanted to make, though he would never fly that close to the sun again.

I watched Boorman and the Devil and The Heretic back to back and came away more convinced than ever that John Boorman is a great director who made a bad, if fascinating film. But that humbling, edifying experience would feed into later-career triumphs like 1984’s Excalibur and 1988’s The General , on which he applied a few of the hard-won lessons he had learned.
As he says of The Heretic with a hint of a smile, “It was very much the film I wanted to make, and I got away with it.”
